analogy.p: A compiler is like a translator who takes a whole written speech away, translates it fully into another language, and hands back a finished document that anyone can read aloud without the translator present. An interpreter is like a live interpreter at a meeting who translates each sentence as the speaker says it, so the translator must be there every time, and who stops the speaker the moment a sentence makes no sense. An assembler is like a person converting abbreviations into full words one by one. The analogy breaks down because a live interpreter handles speech in any order, whereas program lines depend on earlier lines being run first.

bullets: **Source code**: the program the programmer writes, in a high-level language or assembly language.
**Object code / machine code**: the binary instructions the processor can run.
Translator types: **assembler** (assembly language), **compiler** and **interpreter** (high-level languages).
Translators also check the source code for **syntax errors**, because they cannot translate statements that break the rules of the language.
Translation must happen before, or while, the program runs; the way this is done is what separates a compiler from an interpreter.
A program that has been translated into machine code is called an **executable** when it is a file that can be run directly.
core.p: A **translator** is a program that converts **source code** written in a high-level or assembly language into **machine code** that the CPU can execute. The CPU can only understand binary machine code, so without a translator no program written in Python, Java or assembly could run. OCR J277 expects you to know three types of translator: the **compiler**, the **interpreter** and the **assembler**, along with the characteristics of each. Each type is suited to a different language or situation, and you must be able to compare them.

bullets: Translates the **entire program** in one go, then the program is run afterwards as a separate step.
Produces a **stand-alone executable file** of machine code that does not need the compiler to run.
Reports **all the errors** it finds after trying to translate the whole program, usually giving line numbers.
Compiled programs generally **run faster**, because the translation has already been done before running.
The source code is **not given to the user**, which protects the programmer's work and makes it harder to copy or alter.
A compiler may **optimise** the code, rearranging it to run more efficiently.
Each time the source code is changed, it must be **recompiled** before the changes appear in the executable.
core.p: A **compiler** translates the **whole** of the source code into machine code in a single operation, before the program is run. The output is a separate **executable file** (object code) that can be run on its own, as often as needed, without the compiler or the original source code being present. If the compiler finds errors it cannot finish the translation, so it reports the errors it has found (usually as a list, after analysing the entire program) and no executable is produced until they are fixed. Compiled programs are used for most commercial software that is distributed to customers.

bullets: **Advantage**: the executable runs quickly because the program is already in machine code (no translation at run time).
**Advantage**: the user does not need the compiler or source code, so it is easy to distribute and the source code stays secret.
**Advantage**: the whole program is checked for syntax errors before it runs, so the finished product cannot stop at a syntax error in front of the user.
**Disadvantage**: compiling a large program can take a long time, which slows down testing.
**Disadvantage**: errors are reported for the whole program at once, so finding them can be harder, and no part can be run until all syntax errors are fixed.
**Disadvantage**: the executable only runs on the type of computer it was compiled for; the program must be recompiled for each platform.
**Disadvantage**: any change to the code requires recompiling the whole program.
core.p: Because a compiler produces a finished machine code file, the end user gets a fast program that does not need any translation software. The price is paid by the programmer, who must wait for the compile step each time and cannot easily test small changes. The executable is also specific to the type of processor and operating system it was compiled for. Examiners often award marks for linking each advantage to its reason.

bullets: Translates and **executes line by line**, so translation and running happen together.
**No executable file** is produced; the program must be interpreted again each time it is run.
**Stops at the first error** it meets and reports the line, which makes errors easy to locate.
Allows a part of the program to be **tested immediately**, even if the rest is not finished.
The **interpreter must be installed** on the computer running the program.
The user receives the **source code**, so it is less secure and easier to copy or change.
Programs generally **run more slowly** than compiled ones, because each statement is translated every time it executes (even inside a loop).
core.p: An **interpreter** translates and executes the source code **one statement (line) at a time**, as the program runs. It does not create a separate executable file: the machine code is produced in memory and is discarded after use. If an error is found, the interpreter **stops at that line** and reports it, so the programmer can fix the problem immediately and run the program again. The interpreter must be present every time the program is run, and the program is usually distributed as source code.

bullets: **Advantage**: easy to **debug**, because the program stops at the line containing the error.
**Advantage**: can run part-finished programs, so it is good for **testing and learning**.
**Advantage**: no wait for a compile step, so changes can be tried straight away.
**Advantage**: the source code can run on any computer with an interpreter, so it is **portable**.
**Disadvantage**: **slower execution**, because each line is translated every time it is run.
**Disadvantage**: the **interpreter and source code** must be supplied to the user, so the code is not protected.
**Disadvantage**: errors later in the program may not be found until that part is reached, so a program can fail while the user is running it.
core.p: Interpreters suit the development and testing stages, when programmers are writing small parts of code and want instant feedback. The same source code can be run on any computer which has a suitable interpreter, which supports portability. However, the repeated translation makes execution slower, and giving away source code is a security risk. Use these links of 'feature and consequence' when answering questions.

bullets: Input: **assembly language** (mnemonics and labels). Output: **machine code**.
**One assembly instruction = one machine code instruction**, so the translation is direct.
Because assembly is **processor-specific**, an assembler only works for one family of processors.
Produces an **executable** that runs directly on the CPU, like the output of a compiler.
Used when programmers write **low-level code** for embedded systems, device drivers or performance-critical routines.
The assembler also replaces **labels** with memory addresses, which saves the programmer from calculating them.
core.p: An **assembler** translates **assembly language** into machine code. Assembly language uses mnemonics such as LDA and ADD, and each mnemonic corresponds to exactly one machine code instruction, so the assembler converts the program with a **one-to-one** mapping. Assemblers are therefore simpler than compilers, because there is no need to turn one statement into many instructions. The machine code produced only runs on the processor family for which the assembly language was written.

bullets: **Whole program vs line by line**: a compiler translates everything first; an interpreter translates and runs one line at a time.
**Output**: a compiler creates an executable file; an interpreter creates no file.
**Speed of running**: compiled programs run faster; interpreted programs run slower.
**Error reporting**: a compiler gives a list of errors after processing the whole program; an interpreter stops at the first error.
**Distribution**: compiled programs are distributed as executables without source code; interpreted programs need the source and an interpreter.
**Language translated**: compiler and interpreter handle high-level languages; assembler handles assembly language.
**Repeat runs**: a compiled program is translated once and runs many times; an interpreted program is re-translated every run.
core.p: The most common exam question asks you to compare a compiler and an interpreter. A good answer gives paired statements which each mention both translators, and where possible links features to consequences. The assembler is different from the other two because it works on a different language, and the main comparison point is the one-to-one translation. Learn the table in the diagram until you can reproduce it.

bullets: **Developing and testing code**: interpreter, for fast feedback and easy error finding.
**Releasing commercial software** to the public: compiler, to give a fast executable and keep the source code secret.
**Learning to program** (for example in a classroom): interpreter, so students can run code instantly and see where it fails.
**Low-level or embedded code in assembly**: assembler.
A program that must run on **many different types of computer** can be shared as source code, with an interpreter on each, or compiled separately for each platform.

Some systems use **both**: for example Java source code is compiled into an intermediate bytecode, which is then interpreted by a virtual machine (this is extension knowledge, not required for the OCR specification).
core.p: Which translator is better depends on the situation, so exam questions often provide a scenario. During development a programmer often prefers an interpreter because testing is quicker and errors are easy to find. For a final product that will be sold to many customers a compiler is usually better, because it runs faster, it does not need extra software and it protects the source code. Always write the reasoning, not just the name of the translator.

bullets: **Syntax error**: detected by the compiler or interpreter; example: print('hello' with a missing closing bracket.
**Logic error**: not detected by any translator; the output is wrong although the program runs.
**Runtime error**: occurs during execution; an interpreter will stop at that point, and a compiled program will crash when it reaches it.
A compiler reports syntax errors for the whole program, whereas an interpreter reports them one at a time as it reaches them.
Fixing syntax errors does not guarantee the program is correct; it must still be tested with test data.
Error messages from translators usually include the **line number**, which helps the programmer locate the fault.
core.p: Translators detect only certain kinds of error. **Syntax errors** break the rules of the language (for example a missing bracket or a misspelled keyword), and the translator cannot continue until they are fixed. **Logic errors** are mistakes in the program's design, such as using the wrong formula; the translator cannot spot them and the program runs but gives wrong results. **Runtime errors** (such as dividing by zero) happen while the program runs. This links to testing and the Paper 2 topic on defensive design and testing.

bullets: **High-level and low-level languages**: the reason translators are needed, and which translator suits which level.
**IDE tools**: include a translator (and run-time environment) so code can be run and debugged in one place.
**CPU architecture**: the fetch-decode-execute cycle works on machine code, which is what every translator produces.
**Testing and defensive design**: translators find syntax errors; testing finds logic errors.
**Programming techniques**: understanding errors helps in debugging loops, selection and subprograms.
**Software and licensing**: distributing only the executable helps to protect intellectual property (Paper 1 legal topic).
core.p: Translators sit between the languages topic and the IDE topic. The levels of language explain why translation is needed in the first place, and the IDE usually includes a built-in translator along with an editor and error diagnostics. Machine code and the fetch-decode-execute cycle from Paper 1 explain why the output must be binary. Linking these ideas gives richer answers in discuss questions.

exam: **State/Give** (1 mark): 'A compiler translates the whole program at once' is enough for one mark. 'Assembler' alone is correct for 'name the translator for assembly language'.
**Describe how a compiler works** (2 marks): 'translates the whole of the source code into machine code (1) producing an executable file that can be run without the compiler (1)'.
**Describe how an interpreter works** (2 marks): 'translates and executes the program one line at a time (1), stopping when it finds an error (1)'.
**Compare** (4 marks): make each point mention both translators, for example 'An interpreter runs the program line by line whereas a compiler translates all of it first'.

**Give an advantage of a compiler over an interpreter** (1-2 marks): faster execution; the source code is not supplied; the executable does not need the translator installed. Add the reason for the second mark.
**Give an advantage of an interpreter over a compiler**: easier debugging because it stops at the error line; can test part of a program; no compile wait.
**Discuss** (6 marks): consider both translators in the scenario and give a justified conclusion; link 'testing' to interpreters and 'release to customers' to compilers.
Always say **why**: 'faster, because the code is already translated before it is run'.
When asked which translator for assembly code, the answer is **assembler**; a compiler and interpreter are for high-level languages.
Distinguish **source code** and **machine code/object code** clearly; examiners penalise mixing them up.
Look at the scenario clues: 'sold to customers' suggests compiler; 'testing during development' suggests interpreter.

mistakes.r: An interpreter produces no executable; it translates and runs one line at a time each time the program is run.
mistakes.w: An interpreter makes an executable file.

mistakes.r: A compiler translates the whole program in one go, and the executable is then run separately.
mistakes.w: A compiler translates the program line by line.

mistakes.r: The executable is machine code for one type of processor and operating system; the source code is what is portable, and it must be recompiled for each platform.
Interpreters start sooner but run slower, because each statement is translated again every time it is executed. Compiled programs run faster.
mistakes.w: Interpreters are faster because they start straight away.

mistakes.r: A compiler finds syntax errors only; logic errors are not found by a translator and must be found by testing.
mistakes.w: A compiler finds all the errors in a program.

mistakes.r: An assembler translates assembly language only, into machine code, with one assembly instruction becoming one machine code instruction.
Say why: it is easier to debug because it stops at the line with the error; but it needs the interpreter installed and runs slower.
mistakes.w: An interpreter is better because it is easier.

mistakes.r: The executable is in machine code, so the user does not receive the source code and cannot easily read or change it; it is not encryption.
mistakes.w: Compilers are used to protect source code, 'because they encrypt it'.

summary: OCR J277 2.5.1 asks you to know the purpose of translators and the characteristics of an assembler, a compiler and an interpreter, including how each works and the advantages and disadvantages of compilers and interpreters. It matters because it is a regular source of 4 and 6 mark questions and links directly to program development and error finding.

terms.d: A program that converts source code written in a high-level or assembly language into machine code.
A translator that converts the whole of a high-level program into machine code in one go, producing an executable file.
A translator that converts and runs a high-level program one statement at a time, without producing an executable file.
A translator that converts assembly language into machine code, one assembly instruction to one machine code instruction.
The program written by the programmer in a high-level language or assembly language before translation.
The machine code output produced by a translator from source code.
A file of machine code that can be run directly without needing the source code or the translator.
Binary instructions that the CPU can run directly.
A mistake that breaks the rules of the programming language, which prevents the program from being translated.
A mistake in the design of the program that causes it to run but produce incorrect results; translators do not detect it.
An error that occurs while the program is running, such as dividing by zero, causing it to stop.
To rearrange code so that it runs faster or uses less memory; compilers can do this when producing object code.
To run the compiler again on changed source code to produce an updated executable.
Finding and fixing errors in a program.
Able to run on different types of computer with little or no change.

worked.ans: A compiler translates the whole program into machine code at once (1) whereas an interpreter translates and executes one line at a time (1). A compiler produces an executable file that can be run without the translator (1) whereas an interpreter does not produce an executable file and must be present each time the program is run (1).
worked.q: Describe two differences between a compiler and an interpreter. [4]
steps: Choose clear, contrasting features: how much is translated at once, and the output.
Write each as a paired statement, mentioning both translators.

worked.ans: During development an interpreter should be used (1) because it stops at the line with the error, making debugging easier, and parts of the program can be tested without waiting for the whole program to be translated (1). To sell the finished program a compiler should be used (1) because it produces an executable file that runs faster and does not need the customer to have a translator or the source code (1).
worked.q: A programmer is writing and testing a program, then will sell the finished program to customers. Explain which type of translator should be used at each stage. [4]
steps: Development stage: need quick feedback and easy error finding.
Distribution stage: need speed, protecting source code, and no extra software for users.
Name each translator with a reason.

worked.ans: (a) The interpreter translates and runs lines 1 to 499 (1), then stops at line 500 and reports the syntax error (1). (b) The compiler attempts to translate the whole program, reports the error on line 500 (1) and does not produce an executable, so none of the program can be run until the error is fixed (1).
worked.q: A program has 1000 lines and the only error is a syntax error on line 500. Describe what happens when it is run using (a) an interpreter, (b) a compiler. [4]
steps: Interpreter: lines 1 to 499 are translated and run in order.
Reaching line 500, it cannot translate the line, so it stops and reports the error.
Compiler: analyses the entire program before anything runs.
It reports the error and does not produce an executable, so no part of the program runs.
